title: Your Children Hear the Way You Talk About Their Father Too.
paragraphs:
Your Children Hear the Way You Talk About Their Father Too.
You thought you were only telling the truth about what he did. But there was a little heart in the room learning what love sounds like when it is wounded.
She thought he was playing.
That is what made it so easy.
Her little boy was sitting on the floor with two toy cars in his hands, crashing them together, making engine noises under his breath while she stood in the kitchen talking.
She was frustrated.
Maybe she had every reason to be.

Her husband had disappointed her again. Maybe he had forgotten something important. Maybe he had spoken harshly. Maybe he had come home late. Maybe he had left her carrying responsibilities that should never have been hers alone.
And now she needed to tell someone.
So she picked up her phone.
“He never thinks about anybody but himself.”
The little cars kept moving.
“He acts like another child I have to take care of.”
Crash.
“I honestly don’t know why I expected anything different.”
The little boy never looked up.
And because he never looked up, she assumed he wasn't listening.
But children do not have to look at you to hear you.
Sometimes they are building an entire understanding of marriage while sitting quietly on the carpet.
Sometimes they are learning what a husband is from the way their mother describes their father.
Sometimes they are learning what a wife is from the way their father speaks about their mother.
Sometimes they are learning what conflict means before they are old enough to spell the word.
And sometimes the sentences adults call “venting” become bricks children quietly use to build their understanding of love.
That does not mean a mother must pretend her husband never sins.
It does not mean abuse should be hidden.
It does not mean betrayal should be minimized.
It does not mean a woman should remain silent while she or her children are being harmed.

Biblical forgiveness is not permission for continued abuse, and Christian reconciliation never requires pretending evil is good. Serious mistreatment belongs in the light, and wise pastoral, professional, legal, or protective help may be necessary.
This is about something quieter.
More ordinary.
And perhaps because it is ordinary, more easily ignored.
It is about the emotional atmosphere created by our words.
Because your children hear the way you talk about their father too.
And fathers, before you quietly send this article to your wife, keep reading.
Your children hear how you talk about their mother too.
Paul wrote to believers in Ephesus:
“Πᾶς λόγος σαπρὸς ἐκ τοῦ στόματος ὑμῶν μὴ ἐκπορευέσθω…”
Pas logos sapros ek tou stomatos hymōn mē ekporeuesthō…
“Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths…”
—Ephesians 4:29
That Greek word translated “corrupting” is σαπρός — sapros.
It can describe something rotten, spoiled, worthless, or bad.
Paul is not merely teaching Christians to avoid profanity.
He is reaching deeper.
He is confronting speech that carries decay.
Words can do that.
They can bring life into a room.
Or they can bring rot.
Paul continues:
“…ἀλλ’ εἴ τις ἀγαθὸς πρὸς οἰκοδομὴν τῆς χρείας…”
“…but only such as is good for building up, as fits the occasion…”
There is another important word there:
οἰκοδομή — oikodomē.
Building up.
Edification.
The language carries the idea of construction.
And that is an uncomfortable picture when you remember who may be listening.
Because every home is being built with more than lumber, concrete, furniture, and paint.
Homes are built with sentences.
A child hears:
“Your father never does anything right.”
Another brick.
“Your mother is impossible.”
Another brick.
“He is useless.”
Another brick.
“She is crazy.”
Another brick.
“I wish I had never married him.”
Another brick.
“You're just like your father.”
Another brick.
“You're becoming exactly like your mother.”
And suddenly something that sounded like an argument between adults has entered the identity of a child.
That last kind of sentence can cut especially deep.
Because if Daddy is constantly described as worthless, what does a little boy hear when someone says he looks just like Daddy?
If Mommy is constantly described as unbearable, what might a daughter feel when she recognizes her mother's personality in herself?
Children often identify with both parents.
So contempt aimed at a spouse can land somewhere you never intended it to land.
Inside your child.
Maybe that is why this hurts.
Because perhaps you remember being that child.
You remember sitting in the back seat while one parent unloaded anger about the other.
You remember being asked questions you should never have been asked.
“Who do you think is right?”
You remember becoming the messenger.
“Tell your father…”
“Tell your mother…”
You remember learning when to disappear into your bedroom because you could recognize the temperature of the house from the sound of footsteps.
Maybe nobody hit anybody.
Maybe nothing was broken.
But you learned to read silence like a weather forecast.
You knew when a storm was coming.
And perhaps years later, you carried pieces of that emotional climate into your own relationships.
That is why this matters.
Children do not merely learn marriage from the wedding photographs hanging on the wall.
They learn marriage by watching what happens after disappointment.
They watch what Mommy does when Daddy fails.
They watch what Daddy does when Mommy is overwhelmed.
They listen to what parents say when the person they promised to love becomes difficult to love.
And eventually they begin answering enormous questions with tiny observations.
What happens when love gets angry?
What happens when somebody fails?
Do we humiliate them?
Do we recruit other people against them?
Do we keep a record?
Do we weaponize yesterday?
Do we apologize?
Do we forgive?
Do we repair?
Do we pray?
Do we come back to the table?
Do we tell the truth without destroying each other?
This is where the Gospel enters the room.
Not as decoration.
Not as a Christian slogan taped over dysfunction.
As rescue.
Paul does not stop with speech in Ephesians 4.
He keeps going.
“Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and slander be put away from you, along with all malice.”
Then comes the alternative:
“Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you.”
—Ephesians 4:31–32
Look carefully at the foundation.
Paul does not merely say, “Be nicer.”
He anchors forgiveness in something infinitely greater:
“…καθὼς καὶ ὁ Θεὸς ἐν Χριστῷ ἐχαρίσατο ὑμῖν.”
“…as God in Christ forgave you.”
The verb is related to χαρίζομαι — charizomai, carrying the sense of graciously giving or forgiving.
In other words, Christian forgiveness does not begin with pretending the wound was small.
It begins with remembering how enormous grace is.
That changes the entire conversation.
Because Christianity does not tell a wounded wife, “Your pain doesn't matter.”
Jesus never needed darkness renamed as light.
Sin can be called sin.
Betrayal can be called betrayal.
Cruelty can be confronted.
Boundaries can be necessary.
Trust may need to be rebuilt slowly.
Reconciliation requires truth, repentance, and wisdom; forgiveness does not automatically mean immediate restoration of access or trust.
But the Gospel refuses to let another person's sin become permission for ours.
That is the difficult part.
You can be genuinely wounded and still wound others with the way you speak about your wound.
You can be right about what happened and wrong about what you do with it.
You can tell the truth in a way designed to heal.
And you can tell the truth in a way designed to humiliate.
Those are not the same thing.
Perhaps your husband really did fail you.
Perhaps your wife really did disappoint you.
Deal with it.
Speak about it.
Seek wise counsel.
Confront what needs confronting.
Get help where help is needed.
But be careful about turning your children into confidants for burdens their hearts were never designed to carry.
Your daughter does not need to become Mommy's therapist.
Your son does not need to become Daddy's defense attorney.
A child should not have to decide which parent deserves loyalty.
There is something profoundly unfair about asking little shoulders to carry adult resentment.
And perhaps right now you are remembering something you said yesterday.
Or this morning.
Maybe your child was in the next room.
Maybe you saw those little eyes change.
Maybe your teenager became quiet.
Maybe conviction is arriving before you have even finished reading.
Do not run from it.
But do not confuse conviction with hopeless condemnation either.
The Gospel has something better than shame.
Repentance.
Grace.
Repair.
Jesus Christ does not expose sin merely to leave sinners staring at the wreckage.
He calls us to Himself.
At the cross, Christ bore the judgment sinners deserve. In His resurrection is the declaration that sin and death do not get the final word for those who belong to Him.
So maybe tonight the most powerful lesson about marriage your child will ever witness will not be a perfect marriage.
Maybe it will be repentance.
Maybe your child needs to hear:
“Mommy shouldn't have spoken about Daddy that way.”
Maybe:
“Daddy was angry, but what I said about your mother was wrong.”
Maybe:
“You should never feel like you have to choose between us.”
Maybe:
“Adults can disagree without trying to destroy each other's dignity.”
Maybe:
“I sinned with my words, and I asked Jesus to forgive me. I also asked your father to forgive me.”
Think about what that teaches.
Your child learns that authority can apologize.
That Christians do not have to pretend.
That repentance is not humiliation.
That saying “I was wrong” does not make a parent weak.
That grace is not something we only sing about on Sunday.
It belongs in kitchens.
Cars.
Bedrooms.
Text messages.
Arguments.
Apologies.
Marriages.
Families.
This is discipleship.
Not only Bible studies around a table.
Not only family devotionals.
Not only church attendance.
Your child is also being discipled by the way you behave when Scripture becomes inconvenient.
Anyone can quote “be kind to one another” when everyone is getting along.
The verse becomes costly when you are hurt.
Anyone can preach forgiveness when there is nothing to forgive.
The Gospel becomes visible when grace walks into an actual wound without denying the wound.
Your children are watching.
Not because they expect perfection.
They are watching to discover whether Jesus is real enough to change the way people behave when they are angry.
And mother, there is another truth you may need to hear.
Protecting your child's relationship with their father does not require lying for him.
You are not called to manufacture an imaginary man.
You are called to walk in truth.
If he has done something wrong, age-appropriate honesty may be necessary.
But there is a difference between honest explanation and character assassination.
There is a difference between seeking counsel from mature adults and unloading on a child.
There is a difference between saying, “Your father made a wrong choice,” and teaching a child, “Your father is worthless.”
Behavior can be confronted without reducing a human being made in God's image to his worst moment.
And yes, the same truth runs in the opposite direction.
Father, your wife is listening when you speak.
But so are the children.
Sarcasm about their mother teaches something.
Mocking her appearance teaches something.
Calling her emotional, stupid, lazy, crazy, useless, or impossible teaches something.
The joke everybody laughs at may still leave a wound in the child who loves the person you turned into the punchline.
Your home has an emotional vocabulary.
Someone is teaching it.
Maybe both of you are.
So ask yourself something difficult:
If my children eventually speak to their spouses the way I speak to mine, will I be proud of what I taught them?
Sit with that.
Because one day that little boy pushing cars across the floor may become somebody's husband.
One day that little girl coloring at the table may become somebody's wife.
And some of what they believe about conflict may have been learned before they knew they were learning anything at all.
But this story does not have to end in fear.
It can end in grace.
Actually, grace is where the Christian story begins again.
Maybe your home has already heard too many cruel sentences.
Jesus is still able to redeem what sin has damaged.
Maybe apologies are overdue.
Make them.
Maybe counseling is needed.
Seek it.
Maybe bitterness has become so familiar that you have started calling it personality.
Bring it before Christ.
Maybe you have been using your friends, Facebook posts, relatives, or even your children as a courtroom where your spouse is always the defendant and you are always the prosecutor.
Lay down the gavel.
You are not the Savior of your marriage.
Jesus is Lord.
And perhaps before asking Christ to change your spouse, you need to let Him search your own mouth.
Your own heart.
Your own hidden rehearsals of resentment.
“Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths…”
Not because words are insignificant.
Because they are powerful.
“…but only such as is good for building up…”
Build.
Build truth.
Build safety.
Build honesty.
Build repentance.
Build tenderness.
Build a home where conflict can happen without contempt becoming the family language.
Build children who know that disagreement does not require dehumanization.
Build a marriage where apologies are stronger than pride.
And when something has already been torn down?
Let Christ teach you how to rebuild.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Not the polished Christianity where everybody smiles for the family photograph while resentment rots behind closed doors.
The real Gospel.
The Gospel for sinners.
The Gospel for angry mothers.
The Gospel for proud fathers.
The Gospel for wounded spouses.
The Gospel for frightened children.
The Gospel for families who wish they could rewind conversations.
The Gospel for people who cannot undo yesterday but can surrender today to Jesus Christ.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He does not rewrite history by pretending the sin never happened.
He rewrites what happens next.
Repentance can happen next.
Forgiveness can happen next.
Wise boundaries can happen next.
Counseling can happen next.
A changed vocabulary can happen next.
A child hearing, “I was wrong” can happen next.
A husband kneeling before Christ can happen next.
A wife surrendering bitterness can happen next.
A family discovering that grace is more than a church word can happen next.
Maybe somebody you love needs this article.
Not so you can say, “See? This is what you've been doing.”
Please don't weaponize an article about gracious speech.
And if this exposed something in you, do not hide behind a like.
Be honest.
Your honesty may give another struggling believer permission to stop pretending too.
Not because you need another saved post.
Come back to Ephesians 4:29–32 and ask one question before the words leave your mouth:
Am I building right now, or am I spreading decay?
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you grow deeper in Scripture, conviction, repentance, healing, and discipleship, stay close.
If you believe this ministry is worth sustaining, you can do more than consume what it creates.
You can help carry it.
One practical way to glorify God is to steward what He has entrusted to you in ways that help spread His truth.
It is discipleship.
It is helping biblical nourishment keep reaching people.
It is choosing to support a place committed to pointing wounded, wandering, convicted, exhausted, and hungry people back to Jesus Christ.
Not to build our name.
To lift His.
Not because clicking a button earns favor with God—it does not.
But when Christ has given us grace freely, we can freely use our voices, resources, platforms, and influence to help others hear about Him.
Your child may forget what was cooking in the kitchen that night.
They may forget the toy they were holding.
They may forget what everybody was wearing.
But years from now, somewhere inside the marriage they eventually build, they may still hear the language of the home where they first learned what love sounds like when it hurts.

So give them something worth remembering: let them hear that even wounded people can surrender their words to Jesus, even broken conversations can bow before the cross, and even after the sentence you wish you could take back, grace can still write the next one.
